Habermas (“continuation by other means”): 25 August 1956; 8 August 1953
Homo homini homo: June 1957, p. 106, 21 August 1957
I endure, watchful, and I am a vessel For every silence and every storm.
Durando saecula vincit—by enduring, it conquers the ages. ([Virgil,] Georgics II.295)
Curve of Europe with the hieroglyph of the Western world, 11 July 1956 (p. 67)
[Leaf 1r, above the beginning of the text]
Begun: 14 October 1955, aged 67 years, 3 months and 3 days.
Noble simplicity — J. J. Winckelmann’s highly influential definition of classical art.
trahison des clercs — Julien Benda, La trahison des clercs, Paris 1927; German: Der Verrat der Intellektuellen, Munich 1978.
King Peter — Schmitt is presumably referring to Peter II Karađorđević (1923–1970), King of Yugoslavia from 1934. In November 1945 the Communists forced him to give up the throne.
God transforms the lie — Allusion to Romans 1:22 ff.
Enrico Corradini — Italian nationalist writer and journalist (1865–1931); became a minister in 1928.
Sallust contra pecuniam — In his Bellum Iugurthinum (The Jugurthine War), Sallust describes how King Jugurtha was able to bribe the Roman nobility with money.
bellum externum … — Quattuor principes ferro interempti: trina bella civilia, plura externa ac plerumque permixta.
“Four emperors were killed by the sword. There were three civil wars, more foreign wars, and most of them were mixed together.”
Tacitus, Histories I.2. Tacitus is speaking here about the bloody Year of the Four Emperors, AD 69, which was disastrous for Rome.

Otto Brunner — Otto Brunner, Land und Herrschaft, 1973. The first quotation (lines 5–7) is on p. 145; the second (“that the problem of sovereignty …”) is on p. 144, n. 1; and the third (“As long as …”) is also on p. 144. Schmitt’s quotation, however, includes the second word aber (“but”), which is missing here.
Ganahl — Karl-Hans Ganahl (1905–1942), Austrian legal historian.
Willy Haas — Willy Haas, “Eine neue politische Lehre,” in Die literarische Welt (Berlin), vol. 8, no. 12, 20 May 1932, pp. 1–2.

The habilitation thesis by the SS man Lemmel — Herbert Lemmel, Die Volksgemeinschaft, ihre Erfassung im werdenden Recht, Stuttgart/Berlin 1941. Berlin habilitation in law and political science, dated 14 July 1939. Submitted under the title Die Erfassung der Gemeinschaft im lebensgesetzlichen Recht. Reinhard Höhn was the first examiner and Carl Schmitt the second.

See Carl Schmitt, report on the habilitation thesis of Dr. jur. Herbert Lemmel, RW 265 no. 19074; Christian Tilitzki, “Carl Schmitt – Staatsrechtler in Berlin. Einblicke in seinen Wirkungskreis anhand der Fakultätsakten 1934–1944,” in Etappe 7, 1991, pp. 62–117, especially pp. 65–66 and 72–74.
In his habilitation thesis, Lemmel criticized Schmitt’s concepts because they had no connection with “race” or with the “blood-structure of the people.”
The SS officer Lemmel (1911–1990), after returning from Soviet captivity, became a commercial judge in Frankfurt am Main in 1950, and later a businessman and factory owner in Bad Homburg.

Schmitt’s papers contain seven letters and two postcards from Lemmel dating from 1948 to 1978 (RW 0265 nos. 8724–8732), in which Lemmel unsuccessfully tried to establish a closer relationship with Schmitt.

as Ortega told me — Schmitt spoke with the Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset (1885–1955) in Lisbon on 20 May 1944. See Christian Tilitzki, “Die Vortragsreisen Carl Schmitts während des Zweiten Weltkriegs,” in Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 249.
I.1: magna [illa] ingenia cessere — “Those great minds have disappeared.”

I.2: opus adgredior optimum casibus, atrox proeliis, discors seditionibus, ipsa etiam pace saevum — “I approach a work rich in reversals of fortune, savage in battle, divided by sedition, terrible even in peace.”
nefasque mixtum — Conquerar, an moneam mixtum fas omne nefasque?
“Should I lament, or should I warn that good and evil have become completely mixed together?”

Barion essay — Hans Barion, “Der Rechtsbegriff Rudolph Sohms. Zur 100. Wiederkehr von Sohms Geburtstag,” in Deutsche Rechtswissenschaft 7, 1942, pp. 47–51; reprinted in H. Barion, Kirche und Kirchenrecht. Gesammelte Aufsätze, ed. Werner Böckenförde, Paderborn 1984, pp. 115–119.

plenitudo potestatis … — “Immediate absolute power over everyone and over each individual.” This was the formula used from the High Middle Ages onward for the pope’s claim to power. Compare Dictatorship, pp. 42–43.
a Deo excitatus — In Protestant historical writing, Luther was said to have begun his Reformation a Deo excitatus: “called forth by God.”
Berlin lecture — James T. Shotwell (1864–1965), American historian and politician, and a leading promoter of the Kellogg Pact.

The lecture was “Stehen wir an einem Wendepunkt der Weltgeschichte?” (“Are We at a Turning Point in World History?”), given on 1 March 1927 at the German Academy of Politics in Berlin as part of the newly established Carnegie chair. In it, Shotwell called for the renunciation of war.
Published in Henri Lichtenberger / James Shotwell / Max Scheler, Ausgleich als Schicksal und Aufgabe, Berlin 1929, pp. 15–28.
Jäckh — Ernst Jaeckh (1875–1959), journalist, founder and lecturer at the German Academy of Politics; emigrated in 1933.

M. J. Bonn — Moritz Julius Bonn (1873–1965), political economist. In 1919, as director of the Munich School of Commerce, he secured a lectureship there for Carl Schmitt; in 1928 he brought Schmitt to the Berlin School of Commerce.
In his memoirs Bonn wrote very negatively about Schmitt. See M. J. Bonn, So macht man Geschichte. Bilanz eines Lebens, Munich 1953, pp. 330–332, with a note in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 25938.
Spiritus malignus, magnus deceptor — “The evil spirit, the great deceiver.” In Cartesian philosophy, our ability to know is threatened if we mistake what is false for what is true.
Castor-Pollux offer — Refers to the poem “An Levin Schücking” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, final stanza:

Pollux and Castor—alternating glow and pallor, The light of one taken only from the other, And yet the sign of the most faithful loyalty. So give me your hand, my Dioscurus! And may the lovely myth renew itself, Where the twin flame burned above the helmet.
Tout ce qui arrive est adorable — “Everything that happens is worthy of adoration.”
Léon Bloy used the sentence repeatedly, for example in letters to Julien Leclercq dated 31 July 1894 and to Heinrich de Groux dated 8 June 1895, published in L. Bloy, Le mendiant ingrat.

The sentence confirmed Schmitt’s view of history, which had been shaped by Konrad Weiß. Schmitt also liked to quote it as a way of expressing his dislike of unreal “if only” statements about things that had already happened.
Gerhard Günther — (1889–1976), conservative journalist, brother of Albrecht Erich Günther.

The Leviathan has spat me out three times — Namely in 1936, when Schmitt survived an attack by the SS; in 1946, when he was released from the American camp at Berlin-Lichterfelde; and in 1947, when he was released from detention as a witness at Nuremberg.
Quiesco, exsul in patria mea … — “I remain quiet, an exile in my own country.”
The phrase ex[s]ul in patria mea appears often in these years. See the entries for 4 June 1948, 16 September 1949, and 25 November 1949; BW Forsthoff, p. 52; BW Mohler, p. 67; FoP, p. 590.
Its importance to Schmitt’s understanding of himself is clear from the fact that he placed it at the head of Book III of the Glossarium. See the appendix.
Bernanos — Georges Bernanos (1888–1948), French Catholic writer. He was discussed as a possible French ambassador to Rome, but was never appointed. On the speech, see the entry for 13 March 1949.
As he was walking through a street, he saw a young man coming out of a prostitute’s house. The young man blushed deeply when he realized Castruccio had seen him.
“Do not be ashamed when you come out. Be ashamed when you go in.”
Niccolò Machiavelli, Das Leben des Castruccio Castracani von Lucca, German-Italian edition, Cologne/Vienna 1969, p. 81.
“creeping softly” — From Annette von Droste-Hülshoff’s Geistliches Jahr. In the poem “Am zehnten Sonntag nach Pfingsten”:
And let me only look upon A feather, trembling secretly, Remembering that behind its black trace Death and life creep softly.
Pinder — Wilhelm Pinder (1878–1947), art historian; professor at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin from 1935 to 1945.
Fumet — As part of the twenty-volume collected edition of L. Bloy, Stanislas Fumet edited Léon Bloy, Le mendiant ingrat, Paris 1948.
When Schmitt writes “likewise the new edition 1928,” he apparently means this edition.
Claudel — Paul Claudel, Introduction au “Livre de Ruth.” Texte intégral de l’ouvrage de l’Abbé de Moidrey, Paris 1938, pp. 109–110.
Cor Jesu, saturatum opprobriis — “Heart of Jesus, filled with reproaches,” from the Catholic Litany of the Sacred Heart.
already in Bodin — Jean Bodin, Les six livres de la république. Rev. corrigée & augm. de nouveau, Paris 1580 (RW 265 no. 22687).
Bellarmin — Roberto Bellarmino (1542–1621), Jesuit controversial theologian and important cardinal. He developed the doctrine of the Church’s potestas indirecta, its indirect power.
His Autobiografia, written in 1613, was not published until 1751 in Ferrara.
relatiuncula, scriptiuncula, breviculum, notila — Dismissive Latin terms for a “work” or piece of writing: roughly, “little report,” “little writing,” “little brief,” “little note.”
